title: On Birth and Death

inline.s: The original text is excerpted from the Straight Talk on the True Mind.
Death is the dark shadow that hangs over your life, yet it is illusory. Therefore the patriarchs often said:
“One suffers birth and death in vain.”
To break the delusion of

views, the chapter “The True Mind Transcends Death” from the Straight Talk on the True Mind is here excerpted and annotated below. It is hoped that readers will deeply realize and enter into “no birth and death,” and further apply no birth and death in the circumstances of life
[Delusion of views] The confusion of ordinary beings in their views.

[Someone said: I have heard that one who has seen the nature transcends birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of the past were people who had seen the nature, and all had birth and death; and now I see that people in the world who cultivate the Way also undergo birth and death. How can one say they transcend birth and death?]

Someone asked: I have heard that one who has seen the nature transcends birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of the past were people who had seen the nature, and they all had birth and death; and now I see that people in the world who cultivate the Way also have birth and death. How can one say “transcends birth and death”?

[Seeing the nature] To glimpse one's own nature. [One who has seen the nature transcends birth and death] The statement “one who has seen the nature transcends birth and death” is not accurate; it should be: one who has broken attachment to self (for example, an arhat) transcends birth and death. [Attachment to self] Also called attachment to the person, that is, the deluded clinging to body and mind as a self. [Transcending birth and death] This means that after this present span of life ends, the consciousness will not be reborn again, and hence there will be no more death.
For example, one who has realized the fruit of arhatship, when this span of life ends, his consciousness will not be reborn again, but will rest in nirvāṇa (
nirvāṇa with remainder

[Nirvāṇa] The liberated, unconditioned state free from birth and death and free from afflictions. [Nirvāṇa with remainder] When the causes of the birth-and-death of transformation are exhausted, it is called nirvāṇa with remainder; when the fruits of the birth-and-death of transformation are exhausted, and one attains the Buddha's eternal body, it is called nirvāṇa without remainder.
[He answered: Birth and death are originally nonexistent; it is deluded reckoning that makes them exist. It is like a person with an eye disease who sees flowers in the sky
(flowers)

. When a person without the eye disease tells him there are no flowers in the sky, the sick person does not believe it. When the eye disease is gone, the sky-flowers vanish of themselves, and only then does he believe there are no flowers. As long as the flowers have not vanished, those flowers are still empty; it is only that the sick person deludedly clings to them as flowers, not that their substance truly exists.]
Answer: Birth and death are originally nonexistent; it is only through deluded reckoning that they become existent. It is like a person with an eye disease who sees flowers in the sky (
sky-flowers
). A person without the eye disease tells him: there are no flowers in the sky. The sick-eyed person does not believe it. If his eye disease heals, the flowers he sees in the
sky
will naturally vanish as well, and only then does he believe there are no flowers in the sky. Ultimately speaking, the flowers in the
sky
have not been extinguished, because the flowers in the
sky
do not exist at all (having never arisen in the first place
for the reason
, how could one speak of their extinction?). This is merely the hallucination of the sick-eyed person, who believes there are flowers there; they do not truly exist.

[Birth and death are originally nonexistent; it is deluded reckoning that makes them exist] Birth and death are matters within the dream of saṃsāra, and are originally nonexistent. However, ordinary beings deludedly cling to body and mind as a self; therefore after this present span of life ends, they are reborn again, taking on another body. Where there is birth there is bound to be death. If in this life one continues to deludedly cling to body and mind as a self, then after death one must be reborn again, taking on yet another body. Thus birth and death revolve without end. Cultivation is precisely the severing of the attachment to self that deludedly clings to body and mind as a self. Once attachment to self is severed, when this span of life ends, the consciousness will not be reborn again, and there will be no more death.

[It is like a person who deludedly takes birth and death to be existent. When a person without birth and death tells him: birth and death are originally nonexistent — once that person's delusion ceases, birth and death are removed of themselves, and only then does he know that birth and death were originally nonexistent. Even while birth and death have not yet ceased, they are not truly existent; it is merely because one deludedly takes birth and death to be existent.]

Those lost in the dream of saṃsāra deludedly take birth and death to be existent; it is the same principle. When the awakened ones (those without birth and death) tell them: birth and death are originally nonexistent — they will absolutely not believe it. But when they awaken one day (their deluded clinging ceases), birth and death are removed of themselves (they transcend birth and death), and only then do they know that birth and death were originally nonexistent. It is only that while the deluded clinging has not yet ceased, birth and death too are not truly existent; it is simply because of the deluded clinging (like having an eye disease) that there is birth and death (the deluded seeing of sky-flowers).
[The awakened ones] The Song of Realizing the Way says:
“In the dream, plainly there are the six realms; after awakening, vast emptiness — no great thousandfold world.”

Therefore, an arhat's delusions and karma of birth and death being exhausted, he does not receive a further existence (he no longer receives a body in a later life). Thus after their perfect quiescence, there is no more birth and death for them.

[The sutra says: ‘Good man, all sentient beings, from beginningless time, are in all manner of inverted states, like a deluded person who confuses the four directions, deludedly taking the four great elements to be the marks of their own bodies, and the shadow-images of the six sense-objects to be the marks of their own minds. This is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky. And just as the many sky-flowers vanish in empty space, one cannot say there is a definite place of their vanishing. Why? Because there is no place of their arising. All sentient beings, amid that which is unborn, deludedly perceive arising and ceasing, and therefore this is called the revolving of birth and death.’]
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
all sentient beings, from beginning
less
time, are in all manner of inversion, taking illusory appearances for reality,
just as
there is
a person who lost his way, taking north for south
and east for west
likewise
, they deludedly take the body formed of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind to be the marks of a self, and
the thoughts arising from the six sense-organs
in
contact with the six sense-objects
to be the marks of their own mind. This is like
a diseased
eye's blooming, deludedly seeing flowers in the sky. And even
when the diseased eye is healed,
and the many sky-flowers vanish in empty space
it
also
cannot
be
said
that they
have
a
definite
place
of vanishing.
Why is that?
Because they are illusions, and
have no place of
arising
(having never arisen at all, how could there be a place of arising?)
All sentient beings, amid the unborn, deludedly perceive arising and ceasing,
and this deluded perception of arising and ceasing is what is called
the revolving of birth and death.

[Four great elements] All tangible matter in the world is composed of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, and so they are called “great” — namely the great earth, the great water, the great fire, and the great wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture, fire has warmth, and wind has movement. [Shadow-images of the six sense-objects] That is,
the thoughts

arising from the six sense-organs' contact with the six sense-objects. When the six sense-organs contact the six sense-objects, all manner of thoughts arise, and these thoughts are all illusory and unreal; hence they are called the shadow-images of the six sense-objects —
the six sense-organs
contacting the six sense-objects
produce
shadow-images. [Flowers in the sky] That is, flowers in the sky. “Hua” is the ancient form of “hua” (flower).

Question: Why does deludedly taking the four great elements to be the marks of a self, and the shadow-images of the six sense-objects to be the marks of one's own mind, lead to the revolving of birth and death?
Answer: Because all of us sentient beings are within the dream of saṃsāra (on the dream of saṃsāra, see the chapter “The Dream of Ignorance” in
The True Mark of All Dharmas

). If one takes this body (the four great elements) and mind (the shadow-images of the six sense-objects) to be a self (when in fact it is the unborn, unceasing self-nature that is the self), then feelings of love and dislike arise. Then, following these feelings, one creates karma, and through karma receives retribution, so that birth and death revolve without end. If one wishes to leave this dream of birth and death revolving, it must be accomplished through cultivation. The universal path is to sever all afflictions, so that at the time of death one is master of oneself, and can end birth and death and leave saṃsāra. The Chan patriarch Huangbo said in his Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind:
“When ordinary people are on the verge of death, they need only contemplate that the five aggregates
(form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness)

are all empty, that the four great elements have no self, and that the true mind has no marks and neither comes nor goes. At birth, the nature does not come; at death, the nature does not go. Perfectly quiescent, mind and realm are one. If one can thus directly and thoroughly awaken at once, and not be bound by the three times, one is a person who has transcended the world.”
If one practices the Pure Land Dharma gate, one need only maintain the ten recitations at the time of death in continuity (see
The Conditions for Rebirth
), evoke Amitabha Buddha to come and receive one, and so leave the dream of saṃsāra and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Based on this sutra passage, one may trustingly know that one who has reached and awakened to the perfect-enlightenment true mind understands that there is originally no birth and death. Those who now know there is no birth and death, yet cannot escape birth and death, do so because their work is not yet sufficient.]

Based on this sutra passage, it may be known with certainty that one who has reached and awakened to the perfect-enlightenment true mind will understand that there is originally no birth and death (because birth and death are matters within the dream of saṃsāra). Those who already know there is no birth and death (having severed the delusion of views), yet cannot escape birth and death, do so because their work is still insufficient (they have not yet severed the delusion of thought)!

[Trustingly know that one who has reached and awakened to the perfect-enlightenment true mind understands there is originally no birth and death] To know with certainty that one who has reached and awakened to the perfect-enlightenment true mind will understand that there is originally no birth and death. Therefore, for one who has reached and awakened to the perfect-enlightenment true mind, the birth and death of the six realms are indeed illusions. If the deluded clinging
(clinging to body and mind as a self — attachment to self)

ceases, then after their perfect quiescence, the self-nature (consciousness) will not be reborn in the six realms, and they escape birth and death. [Now knowing there is no birth and death] To realize that there is no birth and death is to sever the delusion of views; the cessation of deluded clinging is to sever the delusion of thought. Therefore, to escape birth and death, one must sever the delusions of views and thought. Yet severing the delusions of views and thought is far beyond what ordinary people can accomplish in this present life,

and if one practices the Pure Land Dharma gate, one need only maintain the ten recitations at the time of death in continuity, evoke Amitabha Buddha to come and receive one, and, relying on the Buddha's power, leave the dream of saṃsāra and end birth and death.

[Delusions of views and thought] The delusion of views and the delusion of thought. The delusion of views is the confusion of ordinary beings in their views, such as the five false views of the view of a body, the extreme view, the false view, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions. The delusion of thought is the confusion of ordinary beings in their thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, ignorance, arrogance, and doubt. These two delusions are the root by which sentient beings fall into the three realms and suffer birth and death in vain; severing them brings an end to birth and death and departure from the three realms. For example, in the Śrāvaka vehicle, severing the delusion of views realizes the fruit of stream-entry (Srotāpanna); then, in the process of severing the delusion of thought, there are in order the three stages of the once-returner (Sakṛdāgāmin), the non-returner (Anāgāmin), and the arhat. When the delusion of thought is entirely severed, one realizes the fruit of arhatship and escapes birth and death.

Therefore the scriptures say: Lady Āmra asked Mañjuśrī: ‘Though one clearly knows that birth is an unborn dharma, why is one still carried along by birth and death?’ Mañjuśrī replied: ‘Because one's strength is not yet sufficient.’ Later, the mountain-master Jin asked the mountain-master Xiu: ‘Though one clearly knows that birth is an unborn dharma, why is one still carried along by birth and death?’ Xiu replied: ‘A bamboo shoot will in the end become bamboo, but can it be used as bamboo strips right now?’]
Therefore the scriptures say: Lady Āmra asked Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: ‘Though one clearly knows that birth is an unborn dharma, why is one still carried along by birth and death

’ Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied: ‘This is because the strength to extinguish deluded clinging is not yet sufficient.’ Later, the mountain-master Jin asked the mountain-master Xiu: ‘Though one clearly knows that birth is an unborn dharma, why is one still carried along by birth and death
’ The mountain-master Xiu replied: ‘Although a bamboo shoot will in the end grow into bamboo, can it be split into bamboo strips and used right now?’
[Mountain-master] The master of a mountain, an honorific for the abbot of a monastery.
Though one clearly knows there is no birth and death, one is still carried along by birth and death; this is because
the strength to extinguish deluded clinging
is not yet sufficient, and therefore after death
the self-nature (consciousness)

will again undergo the birth and death of the six realms. Therefore, in study and practice, the cultivation of the strength to extinguish deluded clinging is of the utmost importance. The strength to extinguish deluded clinging consists of two parts: the power of wisdom and the power of concentration. The power of wisdom can know the illusory, and the power of concentration can depart from the illusory. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Know the illusory and you depart at once, without expedient means; depart from the illusory and you are awakened, with no stages.”
Question: How does one cultivate the power of wisdom and the power of concentration?
Answer: Wisdom arises from concentration. Practicing the work of “the myriad thoughts returning to one” and “the one returning to nothingness” (see the chapter “Investigating Present-Moment Chan” in
Aware Chan

) not only cultivates the power of concentration but also cultivates the power of wisdom. In daily life, one must at all times and places use the power of wisdom to know the illusory, and the power of concentration to depart from the illusory, holding concentration and wisdom equally.

[Therefore, to know no birth and death is not as good as to realize no birth and death; to realize no birth and death is not as good as to accord with no birth and death; to accord with no birth and death is not as good as to use no birth and death. People today do not even know no birth and death — how much less realize it, accord with it, and use it? Therefore, those who cling to birth and death do not believe the Dharma of no birth and death — is this not fitting?]

Therefore, to know there is no birth and death is not as good as to realize there is no birth and death; to realize there is no birth and death is not as good as to accord with no birth and death; to accord with no birth and death is not as good as to apply no birth and death in the circumstances of life. People today do not even know there is no birth and death — how much less realize it, accord with it, and apply it in the circumstances of life? Therefore, those who deludedly cling to birth and death do not believe there is no birth and death; this too is understandable!
